title: Global Change: Species on the Move

generated.pipeline: extract → Opus draft → Sonnet accuracy gate → Sonnet fixes

cards.front: Under warming, a range keeps up only by moving as fast as its {{c1::isotherm}}, a line of equal temperature.
cards.quote: Under warming, a range keeps up only by moving as fast as its isotherm, a line of equal temperature.

cards.front: What is climate velocity, and on a mountain, what quantity is the warming rate divided by?
cards.back: The speed of an isotherm: the warming rate divided by how fast temperature changes across the land. On a mountain that is the lapse rate, the drop in temperature with height.
cards.quote: The isotherm's speed, the climate velocity, is the warming rate divided by how fast temperature changes across the land

cards.front: Species moved a median 11 m per decade uphill and 17 km per decade poleward. Why can these raw distances not say which shift kept up with warming?
cards.back: A species is racing its isotherm, not a distance. Each shift must be compared with how fast its own isotherm moved.
cards.quote: Raw distances cannot say, because a species is racing its isotherm, not a distance.

cards.front: If a range started in step with its isotherm, how is its lag after a given time calculated?
cards.back: Lag = (isotherm speed - species speed) x time.
cards.quote: If a range started in step, its lag is the difference in speeds multiplied by the time.

cards.front: Under warming, how can a population persist without shifting its range?
cards.back: Through plasticity, evolution, or cool pockets of habitat.
cards.why: So a range that does not move is not by itself a population that is failing.
cards.quote: a population can also persist without moving, through plasticity, evolution or cool pockets of habitat

cards.front: A species' {{c1::range}} is the area where its populations live and reproduce.
cards.quote: A species' range is the area where its populations live and reproduce.
cards.section: Moving: species shift poleward and uphill

cards.front: Why should a range edge set by temperature move poleward and uphill as climate warms?
cards.back: Temperature falls with latitude and elevation, so the isotherm that marks the edge of tolerable conditions moves poleward and uphill, and the edge should follow it.
cards.quote: if temperature sets the edge of a species' tolerable conditions, part of its niche, the edge should follow its isotherm poleward and uphill
cards.section: Moving: species shift poleward and uphill

cards.front: In Chen and colleagues' meta-analysis of terrestrial range shifts, what pattern linked the shifts to climate, and how strong is that link?
cards.back: Shifts were greatest in studies whose regions had warmed most. That is a correlation across studies, not a manipulation.
cards.quote: Shifts were greatest in studies whose regions had warmed most.
cards.section: Moving: species shift poleward and uphill

cards.front: When Chen and colleagues set each study's shift against its own region's warming, did poleward and uphill shifts keep pace?
cards.back: Poleward shifts on average roughly kept pace; most uphill shifts fell short of what the warming predicted.
cards.quote: poleward shifts on average roughly kept pace, but most uphill shifts fell short of what the warming predicted
cards.section: Moving: species shift poleward and uphill

cards.front: In the BioShifts database, how did poleward shifts of marine species compare with those of terrestrial species?
cards.back: Marine species moved poleward about six times faster; land species lagged further behind their isotherms.
cards.quote: found marine species moving poleward about six times faster than terrestrial ones
cards.section: Moving: species shift poleward and uphill

cards.front: A slope warms 0.3 C per decade, and temperature falls 0.6 C per 100 m of elevation. How fast does the isotherm climb?
cards.back: 0.3 / 0.6 = 0.5 of 100 m per decade = 50 m per decade uphill.
cards.quote: 0.3 C per decade / 0.6 C per 100 m = 0.5 x 100 m = 50 m per decade uphill
cards.section: Keeping pace: climate velocity on a mountain

cards.front: An isotherm climbs 50 m per decade. A species starts in step and moves uphill 11.0 m per decade. What share of the isotherm's shift does it match, and how far behind is it after 30 years?
cards.back: Share: 11.0 / 50 = 22%. Over 3 decades the isotherm moves 150 m and the species 33 m, so it ends 117 m below the elevation that now has its former temperature.
cards.quote: The species ends up 117 m below the elevation that now has its former temperature.
cards.section: Keeping pace: climate velocity on a mountain

cards.front: A mountain warms 0.4 C per decade, and temperature falls 0.5 C per 100 m. A plant starts in step with its isotherm and moves uphill 30 m per decade. What share does it match, and what is its lag after 20 years?
cards.back: Isotherm: 0.4 / 0.5 x 100 m = 80 m per decade. Share: 30 / 80 = 37.5%. Lag: (80 - 30) x 2 decades = 100 m.
cards.why: Assumes constant warming and lapse rate and a range set by temperature alone.
cards.quote: on a mountain that rate is the lapse rate, the drop in temperature with height

cards.front: A species on a warming mountain lags far behind its isotherm. Besides warming, what could explain a real lag?
cards.back: Slow dispersal, cues other than temperature, competitors or predators already upslope, or loss of forest.
cards.quote: A real lag could reflect slow dispersal, cues other than temperature, competitors or predators already upslope, or loss of forest
cards.section: Keeping pace: climate velocity on a mountain

cards.front: Why does climate-driven redistribution change communities rather than moving them intact?
cards.back: Species do not move together, so communities come apart and reassemble, and hosts and pathogens can meet in places they had not shared.
cards.quote: Species do not move together, so communities come apart and reassemble
cards.section: Keeping pace: climate velocity on a mountain

cards.front: {{c1::Phenology}} is the seasonal timing of life-cycle events.
cards.back: A gap opens when a consumer and its food shift by different amounts.
cards.quote: A similar gap can open in phenology, the seasonal timing of life-cycle events, when a consumer and its food shift by different amounts
cards.section: Keeping pace: climate velocity on a mountain

cards.front: Both, Visser and colleagues compared pied flycatcher declines across Dutch forests with early or late caterpillar peaks. Why does the contrast support but not establish that timing affects population size?
cards.back: It was observational: forests were not assigned, and the cross-site caterpillar peaks were measured in a single year.
cards.quote: the contrast supports, but does not by itself establish, a causal effect of timing on population size
cards.section: Timing: phenology and mismatch

cards.front: {{c1::Density dependence}} is a rate, such as first-winter survival, that changes with the number of animals.
cards.back: So a loss at the nest can be made up later.
cards.quote: a rate, here first-winter survival, that changes with the number of animals
cards.section: Timing: phenology and mismatch

cards.front: In a great tit population, mismatch with the caterpillar peak lowers the number of young that fledge. Predict whether population growth must fall, and why.
cards.back: Not necessarily. In years when few young were produced, more survived their first winter, so population growth showed no detectable effect.
cards.why: Density dependence: survival rises when numbers are low, offsetting the loss at the nest.
cards.quote: yet more of those young survived their first winter in years when few were produced
cards.section: Timing: phenology and mismatch

cards.front: Great tits were kept for six years in aviaries with warm and cold temperature patterns 4 C apart. What was the result?
cards.back: The warm treatment advanced laying in five of the six years; that temperature is the cue is the authors' reading.
cards.quote: the warm treatment advanced laying in five; the cue is the authors' reading
cards.section: Timing: phenology and mismatch

cards.front: Which driver do reviews such as the IPBES global assessment name as the largest single driver of the decline in land biodiversity?
cards.back: Habitat loss to land use: converting forest and grassland to farms, pasture and towns.
cards.quote: name this habitat loss as the largest single driver of the decline in land biodiversity
cards.section: The other drivers: land, aliens, acid and nitrogen

cards.front: Newbold and colleagues' global model estimated what change in within-sample species richness from land use and related pressures?
cards.back: An average fall of 13.6%, and 76.5% in the worst-affected habitats. These are model estimates from sampled sites.
cards.quote: reduced within-sample species richness by an average of 13.6%, and by 76.5% in the worst-affected habitats
cards.section: The other drivers: land, aliens, acid and nitrogen

cards.front: On a mountain where the lower slopes were recently cleared for pasture, a beetle moved uphill faster than its isotherm. Does the shift show that warming alone moved it?
cards.back: No. Across 43 sites, forest loss in warmer regions went with faster upslope movement, so land use may drive part of the shift.
cards.why: That finding is a correlation across sites; a study must measure land cover to separate the two drivers.
cards.quote: An uphill shift is not by itself proof that climate acted alone.
cards.section: The other drivers: land, aliens, acid and nitrogen

cards.front: An {{c1::alien species}} is one moved by people beyond its native range.
cards.quote: An alien species is one moved by people beyond its native range
cards.section: The other drivers: land, aliens, acid and nitrogen

cards.front: Using IUCN Red List data, how did alien species rank among threats associated with plant and vertebrate extinctions since 1500?
cards.back: Second most common threat overall, and the most common for vertebrates.
cards.quote: alien species were the second most common threat associated with plant and vertebrate extinctions since 1500, and the most common for vertebrates
cards.section: The other drivers: land, aliens, acid and nitrogen

cards.front: A plot of first records of established alien species rises steeply after 1970. Does the curve show that arrivals rose by that much?
cards.back: Not by itself. A first record can lag the real introduction, so the curve tracks detection as well as arrival.
cards.quote: a first record can lag the real introduction, so that curve tracks detection as well as arrival
cards.section: The other drivers: land, aliens, acid and nitrogen

cards.front: Net reaction of ocean acidification: CO2 + H2O + {{c1::CO3 2-}} → 2 HCO3-
cards.back: Dissolved CO2 uses up carbonate ion.
cards.quote: Net: CO2 + H2O + CO3 2- → 2 HCO3-
cards.section: The other drivers: land, aliens, acid and nitrogen

cards.front: How does dissolving more CO2 in seawater make it harder for calcifiers to build calcium carbonate shells?
cards.back: Carbonic acid releases hydrogen ions, which lower pH and combine with carbonate, so carbonate is used up and the saturation state of calcium carbonate falls.
cards.quote: the acid's hydrogen ions lower pH and use up the carbonate that shells are built from
cards.section: The other drivers: land, aliens, acid and nitrogen

cards.front: What does a calcium carbonate saturation state above 1 versus below 1 mean?
cards.back: Above 1, forming the mineral is chemically favoured; below 1, unprotected calcium carbonate tends to dissolve.
cards.why: Organisms differ; their calcification has no universal threshold at 1.
cards.quote: above 1, forming the mineral is chemically favoured; below 1, unprotected calcium carbonate tends to dissolve
cards.section: The other drivers: land, aliens, acid and nitrogen

cards.front: Surface seawater stays above pH 7 as it absorbs CO2. Why is the process still called acidification?
cards.back: The word names the direction of change, falling pH, not an acidic end state.
cards.quote: Surface seawater stays alkaline, above pH 7, while this happens; "acidification" names the direction of change.
cards.section: The other drivers: land, aliens, acid and nitrogen

cards.front: Eighteen species of sea-floor calcifiers are held at controlled CO2 levels up to about ten times pre-industrial. Predict whether every species calcifies less.
cards.back: No. More than half calcified less, several calcified more and one did not respond.
cards.why: The same spread the syntheses found: responses differ widely between groups.
cards.quote: More than half calcified less, several calcified more and one did not respond
cards.section: The other drivers: land, aliens, acid and nitrogen

cards.front: Nitrogen often limits plant growth. On Minnesota prairie with ambient deposition of 6 kg N per hectare per year, predict the effect of adding 10 kg N per hectare per year on plant species number.
cards.back: It fell, by 17% relative to controls.
cards.why: In a second experiment, species number recovered a decade after additions stopped, but abundances had not.
cards.quote: found that the addition reduced plant species number by 17% relative to controls
cards.section: The other drivers: land, aliens, acid and nitrogen

cards.front: Why can adding a nutrient such as nitrogen reduce plant diversity?
cards.back: It tends to reinforce the dominance of a few species, which win a limiting resource such as light or water; soil acidification adds a further route.
cards.quote: Added nitrogen tends to reinforce the dominance of a few species
cards.section: The other drivers: land, aliens, acid and nitrogen

cards.front: Fertilized plots of a grassland lose plant species. Design a test of whether competition for light causes the loss, and say what result would implicate light.
cards.back: Add light to the understory in fertilized and unfertilized plots. If added light prevents the loss in fertilized plots, competition for light is implicated. If not, test other routes such as water or soil acidification.
cards.why: Rests on the light-addition experiment; neither light nor water is a universal mechanism.
cards.quote: added light to the understory and prevented the loss caused by fertilization, which implicates competition for light
cards.section: Why nitrogen cuts diversity: light, water and soil

cards.front: In studies of biological change, what does detection show, and what does it not show?
cards.back: That a change happened beyond what chance or natural variation would produce; not what caused it.
cards.quote: Detection shows that a change happened beyond what chance or natural variation would produce, not what caused it.
cards.section: How strong is the attribution?

cards.front: What two links does attributing a biological change to human-caused warming require?
cards.back: From the biological change to regional warming, then from regional warming to human causes, while assessing plausible alternatives.
cards.quote: from the biological change to regional warming, then from regional warming to human causes
cards.section: How strong is the attribution?

cards.front: A model reports that a frog's range will shrink 30% by 2080 under a high-emissions scenario. Is this detection, attribution or projection, and what is its status?
cards.back: Projection: a conditional result under a stated scenario, not an observation of the future.
cards.quote: Projection is what a model gives under a stated scenario of emissions or land use.
cards.section: How strong is the attribution?

cards.front: A statistical model of range shifts includes warming and forest loss as covariates. What can it and can it not rule out?
cards.back: It can expose a confounder it measured, but not one it did not measure.
cards.why: Unlike a manipulation, it does not assign the driver.
cards.quote: can expose a confounder it measured but not one it did not
cards.section: How strong is the attribution?

cards.front: Why do global summaries of range shifts and observed biological changes describe a biased sample?
cards.back: The data are concentrated in Europe and North America, the developed regions of the Northern Hemisphere.
cards.quote: the BioShifts range records are likewise biased toward the developed regions of the Northern Hemisphere
cards.section: How strong is the attribution?

cards.front: Over 25 years a bird's laying date advanced 6 days while its caterpillar prey's peak advanced 15 days. By how much did the offset change, and what fraction of the prey's shift did the bird match?
cards.back: Offset changed by 15 - 6 = 9 days; the bird matched 6 / 15 = 40% of its prey's shift.
cards.why: Laying date stands in for peak demand only if the time from laying to hungry nestlings stays the same.
cards.quote: the prey peak moved 20 - 10 = 10 days more than laying, so the offset changed by 10 days
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: A declining songbird has a growing mismatch with its prey. Vital-rate data show breeding success and nestling survival unchanged, while adult survival on the wintering grounds fell sharply. Is mismatch the likely main cause?
cards.back: Unlikely. Mismatch should show up mainly in breeding success and survival of young; a decline explained by adult winter survival points elsewhere.
cards.why: Carry-over effects, where one season affects the next, can blur that line.
cards.quote: If a fall in adult survival on the wintering grounds explains most of the decline, mismatch is unlikely to be the main cause
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Many populations of a bird face prey peaks of different timing. If mismatch drives decline, what pattern across populations is predicted, and what experiment could test food timing directly?
cards.back: Decline should be steepest where the gap between laying and prey peak is largest. Supplementary feeding after the natural peak tests whether food timing limits breeding success.
cards.quote: If mismatch matters, decline should be steepest where the gap is largest.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: A study convincingly shows that mismatch drove a bird population's decline. What further evidence is needed to attribute the decline to human-caused warming?
cards.back: Evidence that the local spring warming is itself attributable to human forcing; otherwise the decline is attributed to timing only.
cards.why: The second link of joint attribution.
cards.quote: that needs evidence that the local spring warming is itself attributable to human forcing
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Between two stations, mean temperature falls about 0.4 C per 100 km poleward, and the lapse rate is 0.6 C per 100 m. About how many km poleward match one metre uphill?
cards.back: 1 m uphill = 0.006 C; 0.006 / 0.004 C per km = about 1.5 km poleward.
cards.why: Not a general conversion: each study should use its own local gradient.
cards.quote: one metre uphill matches about 1.5 km poleward there
cards.section: One metre uphill, in kilometres poleward

cards.front: Using 0.6 C per 100 m uphill and 0.4 C per 100 km poleward, what temperature change does each of Chen and colleagues' medians, 11.0 m per decade uphill and 17 km per decade poleward, track?
cards.back: Uphill: 11.0 x 0.006 = about 0.066 C per decade. Poleward: 17 x 0.004 = about 0.068 C per decade. Both roughly 0.07 C per decade.
cards.why: So the medians alone cannot say which shift kept up; each needs its region's warming.
cards.quote: On these figures Chen and colleagues' two medians each track roughly 0.07 C per decade.
cards.section: One metre uphill, in kilometres poleward

cards.front: Warming is 0.3 C per decade on a mountain with a lapse rate of 0.6 C per 100 m, and on a lowland where temperature falls 0.4 C per 100 km poleward. Using these illustrative figures, compare the two climate velocities and what they demand of species.
cards.back: Mountain: 0.3 / 0.6 x 100 m = 50 m per decade. Lowland: 0.3 / 0.4 x 100 km = 75 km per decade. The units differ (m vs km), so each speed is judged against a species' own shift; the 0.4 C per 100 km gradient is illustrative, not general. A shallow gradient makes the isotherm move far faster, so lowland species must travel much farther to keep pace.
cards.why: Climate velocity = warming rate / spatial temperature gradient.
cards.quote: The isotherm's speed, the climate velocity, is the warming rate divided by how fast temperature changes across the land
